subject: physics

moments.title: Cherenkov sees the glow
moments.body: Cherenkov, a Soviet graduate student, notices a faint blue glow when radium emits radiation into water. The glow comes from charged particles travelling faster than light in the medium (though not faster than light in vacuum).
moments.takeaway: Particles can travel faster than light — in water.

moments.title: Frank and Tamm explain
moments.body: Frank and Tamm derive the theory: when a charged particle exceeds c/n in a medium, it emits an electromagnetic shockwave — the optical analogue of a sonic boom.
moments.takeaway: Cherenkov radiation is the light equivalent of a sonic boom.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body: The three share the 1958 Nobel. Cherenkov detectors become standard in particle physics for identifying high-speed particles by their characteristic ring of light.
moments.takeaway: Cherenkov detection is now a workhorse of particle physics.

moments.title: Super-Kamiokande and IceCube
moments.body: Super-Kamiokande (50,000 tonnes of water) and IceCube (a cubic km of Antarctic ice) detect Cherenkov light from neutrino interactions. SN 1987A neutrinos and TeV cosmic neutrinos are caught this way.
moments.takeaway: Cherenkov rings reveal the neutrino sky.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Cherenkov radiation is used in IACT (Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes), particle accelerators, nuclear reactors (the iconic blue glow), and astroparticle physics. CTA, a next-generation Cherenkov array, is under construction in Spain and Chile.
now.open_questions: What are the sources of PeV cosmic neutrinos?

reflection: Cherenkov nearly didn't believe his own observation. He repeated it for years before publication. When should you doubt a clear experimental result?
